overview: This bill, called the Working Families Flexibility Act, would let private-sector workers choose paid time off instead of overtime pay, an option government employers already have. For five years, an eligible worker who put in overtime could take 1.5 hours of "comp time" off for each overtime hour instead of time-and-a-half pay, but only through a union contract or a written, voluntary agreement that cannot be a condition of the job. Workers could save up to 160 hours, could ask to cash out unused time at any point, and must be paid for unused time at the end of each year or when they leave the job. Employers could not pressure workers to take or use comp time and would owe damages if they did, and workers must be allowed to use their time off within a reasonable period unless it unduly disrupts the business. As of February 12, 2026, a House committee had approved it and it was awaiting a vote by the full House.
for: Supporters say many workers would value extra time off for family needs more than extra pay, and the bill makes the choice voluntary with safeguards and a guaranteed cash-out.
against: Critics say workers may feel pressured to accept comp time, effectively lending their overtime pay to the employer, and may not be able to take the time off when they actually need it.
